subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If x^(log y) = log x, show that dy/dx = (y/x)[(1 − log x log y)/(log x)²].

mark_split.label: Differentiate both sides with respect to x

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.206, chapter 9 DIFFERENTIATION, Long Answer question 6. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. It was also checked numerically: solving the relation for y gives y = exp(log(log x)/log x), and the printed formula agrees with a central difference quotient of that function at x = 3 (0.272567037) and at x = 5 (0.054390375), to nine decimal places at both points.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say what you do to both sides first, and what the right side turns into.

steps.label: Take logarithms of both sides
steps.margin_note: First two marks. The left side has a variable base and a variable power, so it needs the logarithm. Do not forget that the right side is then log(log x), not log x.
steps.memory_tip: Taking a logarithm of log x gives log(log x). Write it as a whole bracket so it is not read as (log x) again.
lines: The left side has x in the base and log y in the power, so neither the power rule nor the exponential rule applies. Take logarithms of both sides.
This needs x > 1, so that log x is positive and log(log x) exists, and y > 0.

recall.must_convey: That logarithms are taken on both sides, giving log y · log x = log(log x).
accept: take log on both sides so the power log y comes down
log y into log x equals log of log x
the right side becomes log of log x, not log x
variable base and variable power so take logarithms
rendu vaipulaki log teesthe log y log x equals log log x
the power comes down in front as log y

steps.why: The logarithm brings the power log y down in front, turning the left side into a product that the product rule can handle. The right side must be logged as well, which is what produces log(log x).
common_mistakes: Leaving the right side as log x after taking logarithms of the left side.
Writing log[x^(log y)] as (log x)^(log y), which keeps the power where it was.

steps.label: Differentiate both sides with respect to x
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The left side is a product, so the product rule is used, and log y carries a dy/dx. The right side needs the chain rule twice over, giving 1/(x log x).
steps.memory_tip: The derivative of log(log x) is one over the inside, times the derivative of the inside: (1/log x) × (1/x).

recall.must_convey: That the left side is differentiated by the product rule with a dy/dx on log y, and the right side gives 1/(x log x).
accept: product rule on the left, chain rule on the right
log x into one by y dy by dx plus log y by x
the derivative of log of log x is one by x log x
every derivative of y brings a dy by dx
log log x derivative one by x log x avuthundi
left side product rule, right side one over x log x

steps.why: y is a function of x, so log y differentiates to (1/y)(dy/dx). On the right, log(log x) is a function of a function, so the chain rule gives one over the inner function times the inner derivative.
common_mistakes: Writing the derivative of log(log x) as 1/(log x) and leaving out the 1/x.
Differentiating log y as 1/y without the dy/dx factor.

steps.label: Make dy/dx the subject
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Only one term carries dy/dx, so there is nothing to collect — move the other term across and multiply by y/log x.
steps.memory_tip: One dy/dx term only, so this is a one-move rearrangement: shift, then multiply by the reciprocal of what stands in front.
lines: From (2),  (log x / y)(dy/dx) = 1/(x log x) − (log y)/x
Multiplying both sides by y/log x,

recall.must_convey: That the term without dy/dx is moved across and both sides are multiplied by y/log x.
accept: shift log y by x to the right side
multiply both sides by y over log x
only one term has dy by dx so nothing needs collecting
dy by dx equals y by log x times the bracket
log y by x ni avatali pampi y by log x tho multiply cheyyali
make dy by dx alone on the left
heard_as: multiply by y over log x

steps.why: Unlike the other implicit questions in this chapter, dy/dx appears in only one term here, so no collecting is needed. That is worth noticing before writing anything: it saves a whole line of work.
common_mistakes: Multiplying only one of the two terms in the bracket by y/log x.
Keeping the minus sign on the wrong term after the shift.

steps.label: Simplify to the printed form
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Take 1/x out of the bracket first, then put what is left over the single denominator log x. The two log x factors then meet and give (log x)².
steps.memory_tip: Pull 1/x out first. What remains is 1/log x − log y, and over one denominator that is (1 − log x log y)/log x.
lines: Taking 1/x out of the bracket in (3),
= (y/x) · (1/log x) · (1 − log x log y)/(log x)

lines.text: ∴ dy/dx = (y/x)[(1 − log x log y)/(log x)²]

recall.must_convey: That 1/x is taken out and the bracket is written over log x, so the two log x factors give (log x)² in the denominator.
accept: take one by x outside the bracket first
one by log x minus log y becomes one minus log x log y over log x
the two log x factors give log x squared at the bottom
the answer is y by x into one minus log x log y over log x whole squared
log x rendu sarlu vachi log x square avuthundi
put the bracket over a common denominator log x
heard_as: one minus log x log y

steps.why: The question states the answer, so the marks are for reaching that exact form. The (log x)² appears only when the log x already in front is multiplied by the log x brought in by the common denominator.
common_mistakes: Stopping at (y/log x)[1/(x log x) − (log y)/x], which is correct but is not the form asked for.
Writing (log x)² as log(x²), which is a different quantity.

insider_note: Take logarithms of both sides to reach (log y)(log x) = log(log x), which needs x > 1. Then differentiate implicitly, treating log y as the unknown function.
